A 55-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with a chief complaint of weight loss.

At admission and during hospitalization, weight loss, thirst, constipation, and numbness were noted. His medical history included diagnoses of hypertension, herpes zoster, and lung cancer. His family history included cataracts in his grandmother.

Investigations and assessment after admission confirmed heart failure. Atrial fibrillation was also suspected, and he remains under observation.

During hospitalization, appropriate management of heart failure was provided, and improvement in symptoms was confirmed.

At discharge, weight loss, thirst, constipation, and numbness were present, but there were no major changes affecting his vital prognosis, and his clinical course was favorable.

No discharge medications were documented.

The plan is to continue management of heart failure in the outpatient setting. In addition, considering the possibility of atrial fibrillation, further investigations will be performed as needed.

As part of nursing care, the bed rails were raised to ensure safety, intravenous access was established, and oxygen administration was initiated. In response, the patient showed a tendency toward reduced anxiety, but fluctuations in his level of consciousness persisted. Monitoring of vital signs and assessment of his level of consciousness continued, and preparations were made to report to the physician.

A 46-year-old woman was admitted with a chief complaint of tremor. Physical findings on admission included tremor, pruritus, and shortness of breath. No dizziness was observed, and there was no nausea.
Treatment Course
After admission, chest X-ray and chest CT were performed, revealing infiltrates in the lung fields, and pneumonia was diagnosed. Intravenous antibiotic infusion therapy was initiated to improve her symptoms. In addition, she complained of discomfort during urination and upper abdominal pain, prompting urine culture and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. Although bacterial growth was confirmed on urine culture, a definitive diagnosis was not established, and she remains under observation for suspected cystitis. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy also revealed an ulcerative lesion in the gastric body, suggesting a possible gastric ulcer.
Condition at Discharge
Currently, tremor, pruritus, and shortness of breath are improving. No dizziness was observed, and there was no nausea.
Discharge Prescriptions
Antibiotics and gastric mucosal protective agents were prescribed, and outpatient follow-up was instructed.
Future Plan
She was instructed to continue monitoring for symptoms of cystitis and gastric ulcer after discharge. Urinalysis and reassessment of her gastric condition are planned at the next outpatient visit.

An anomalous course of the hepatic artery is observed at a high frequency of 25 to 45%.
We report a patient with gastric cancer who had an anomalous course of the common hepatic artery, which branched normally from the celiac artery, passed dorsal and caudal to the portal vein, and emerged ventrally from the right side of the portal vein.
The patient was a 76-year-old man.
His history included open cholecystectomy and EMR for early ascending colon cancer.
Total gastrectomy, splenectomy, D2 dissection, and Roux-Y reconstruction were performed for gastric cancer of the lesser curvature of the upper gastric body (type 5, T3, N1, P0, H0, CY0, M0, Stage IIB).
At that time, the common hepatic artery was confirmed to run dorsal and caudal to the portal vein toward the liver.
Postoperative review confirmed the same findings on contrast-enhanced CT.
The diversity of an anomalous course of the hepatic artery is thought to arise embryologically through the development and regression of longitudinal and transverse interarterial anastomotic branches among the four basic mesenteric arteries of the upper abdomen (left gastric artery, hepatic artery, splenic artery, and superior mesenteric artery).
Development of the portal vein and rotation of the gastrointestinal tract produce further diversity, and the course is formed and completed at approximately 4 to 10 weeks of gestation.
In this case, during No. 8a lymph node dissection along the superior border of the pancreatic head and body, the portal vein appeared before the common hepatic artery, which normally serves as a landmark, making it impossible to distinguish No. 8a from 8p; both were therefore resected en bloc.
However, it was difficult to determine how far the dorsal approach could safely be extended, and the possibility that dissection at this site was inadequate cannot be excluded.

Findings of metastatic adenocarcinoma were observed, prompting an investigation, but the primary site was unknown. Her symptoms gradually worsened, and she died on October 3.

【Introduction】We report a case of a young woman who underwent partial small bowel resection through a mini-laparotomy after IVR for gastrointestinal bleeding associated with abnormal blood vessels in the small intestine.
【Case】A 27-year-old woman.
No past medical history.
In December 2012, she developed severe abdominal pain and passage of blood per rectum and was transported to our emergency department.
Small bowel bleeding was diagnosed on contrast-enhanced abdominal CT.
She was in a state of hemorrhagic shock on arrival and received a transfusion of 8 units of packed red blood cells.
Emergency IVR was performed to identify the bleeding source and achieve hemostasis.

[Objective] In early 2019, sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (SOF/VEL) became available in Japan for the first time for decompensated hepatitis C cirrhosis, providing more patients with an opportunity for viral eradication. However, because these patients have numerous complications of cirrhosis, greater attention than ever is considered necessary to the occurrence of adverse events during treatment.
Therefore, the objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of treatment in patients who started SOF/VEL at our hospital.
[Methods] We examined the clinical backgrounds and treatment courses of six patients with decompensated hepatitis C cirrhosis who started SOF/VEL at our hospital.
[Results] Of the six patients who started SOF/VEL, two were men and four were women.
The median age was 68 years (52–81 years).
All patients had Genotype 1b and no history of DAA treatment.

Her CPS score was 10.

She developed sepsis due to cellulitis on the same day that SOF/VEL administration was started.

[Conclusion] Although SOL/VEL has high antiviral efficacy, patients with decompensated cirrhosis are prone to changes in their clinical condition, and meticulous attention is required when monitoring their course during treatment.

[Background] Balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration of gastric varices (B-RTO) is frequently performed in Japan to treat gastric varices associated with cirrhosis and is also recommended in the 2015 clinical practice guidelines for cirrhosis.
Meanwhile, partial splenic embolization (PSE) is a treatment that can reduce splenic volume, correct hypersplenism, and improve portal pressure and liver function by partially embolizing the splenic artery.
We report a case of alcoholic cirrhosis with gastric varices accompanied by massive splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia, in which PSE was performed as initial treatment, followed by elective B-RTO, resulting in improvement in gastric varices and liver function.
[Case] A man in his 70s.
While receiving treatment for alcoholic cirrhosis from a local physician, he was referred to our department in year X for treatment of esophageal varices.
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed esophageal varices (Lm, F3, Cb, RC0) and gastric varices (Lg-cf, F1, RC0). Endoscopic injection sclerotherapy was performed, and regression of the esophageal varices was observed; therefore, he was followed as an outpatient.
Regular upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and abdominal imaging during outpatient follow-up showed no worsening of the esophageal varices, but gradual enlargement of the gastric varices (F1 → F2) was observed.
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT revealed massive splenomegaly and a splenorenal shunt, as well as gastric varices protruding into the gastric lumen.
Furthermore, a low platelet count associated with hypersplenism (50,000–70,000/μl) and hyperammonemia (approximately 100 mg/dl) were also observed. Therefore, the plan was to first improve splenic function with PSE and then treat the gastric varices with B-RTO.
In year X+3, PSE was performed to embolize approximately 80% of the entire spleen, primarily targeting the inferior polar branches of the splenic artery. The platelet count, which was 73,000/μl before treatment, rose to 158,000/μl approximately 1 month later, indicating a favorable improvement in hypersplenism.
Subsequently, B-RTO was performed on the gastrorenal shunt draining into the left adrenal vein. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed disappearance of blood flow to the gastric varices, and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy approximately 2 months later showed reduction in the size of the gastric varices (Lg-cf, F1, RC0). Improvement in liver function was observed, with a platelet count of 150,000/μl and an ammonia level of 32 mg/dl, among other findings.
[Discussion and Conclusion] For gastric varices associated with cirrhosis with markedly increased splenic function, these findings suggested the possibility that performing PSE first allows B-RTO to be performed more safely and may ultimately improve liver function.

In patients who have undergone hepatic portoenterostomy for biliary atresia, gastrointestinal bleeding, including rupture of gastroesophageal varices, is often difficult to control because of severe portal hypertension.
Even in patients who have not developed liver failure, refractory, massive gastrointestinal bleeding is one of the important indications for liver transplantation in biliary atresia.
We reviewed cases in which gastrointestinal bleeding could not be controlled and liver transplantation was performed within 1 month of bleeding.
Of the 1,411 patients who underwent liver transplantation at our hospital from June 1990 through the end of August 2010, 550 had biliary atresia, and 136 of these had gastrointestinal bleeding among their indications.
Of these, 26 patients whose bleeding could not be controlled and who underwent liver transplantation within 1 month were included in the study.
Age at transplantation ranged from 0 years 8 months to 14 years 8 months (mean, 4 years 2 months), and the male-to-female ratio was 10:16.
The bleeding sites were small intestinal bleeding in 10 patients, rupture of gastroesophageal varices in 6 patients, bleeding from both sites in 6 patients, and an unknown bleeding site in 4 patients.
For bleeding from esophageal varices, endoscopic treatments such as sclerotherapy and ligation are performed first; liver transplantation is indicated in patients who have repeated rebleeding despite these treatments and in whom hemostasis cannot be achieved even with an S-B tube.
Small intestinal bleeding frequently involves bleeding from the Roux-en Y limb, including the enterostomy site, and treatment is difficult even with angiography; liver transplantation is indicated when hemostasis cannot be achieved even with conservative treatment consisting of fasting and blood transfusion.
During liver transplantation for portal hypertension, particularly in small children, if sufficient blood flow through the main portal vein cannot be obtained, collateral vessels such as the coronary vein and spleno-renal shunt are dealt with, and blood flow to the retroperitoneum is additionally interrupted to secure portal blood flow.
In bleeding from the Roux-en Y limb, the collateral vessels that are the source of bleeding can be dealt with by separating the intestine from the liver.
The postoperative course was relatively favorable, and 21 of the 26 patients (81%) were alive, including children who had been in a preshock state because of preoperative bleeding.

We report a case of acute-onset hepatic encephalopathy without underlying liver disease, in which an intrahepatic portal-hepatic venous shunt was diagnosed and percutaneous transhepatic obliteration (PTO) was performed.
[Case] The patient was a 68-year-old man.
During treatment for myocardial infarction, a tendency toward somnolence was noted, and blood tests revealed hyperammonemia (193 μg/dL).
T1-weighted head MRI showed high signal intensity in the bilateral globus pallidus, and impaired consciousness due to hepatic encephalopathy was diagnosed. A congenital metabolic disorder or a similar condition was suspected, and he was referred to our hospital.
There was no history of alcohol consumption.
HBs antigen was negative, and HCV antibody was negative.
At transfer, ammonia was 176 μg/dL, the Fischer ratio was 1.4 (reference range, 2.43–4.4), and blood citrulline was 27.8 nmol/mL (reference range, 17.1–42.6 nmol/mL).
Abdominal ultrasonography showed no abnormalities in liver morphology but showed dilation of a left portal vein branch, and Doppler examination suggested a portal-hepatic venous shunt.
Contrast-enhanced CT showed only an intrahepatic shunt, with no extrahepatic shunt observed.
The dose of lactitol, which had been initiated at the previous hospital, was increased, but because it had little effect, PTO was performed.
Portal venography revealed innumerable nondilated shunts in both lobes, in addition to the shunt in the left portal vein branch identified on CT.
The aneurysmal portal-hepatic venous shunt in the left portal vein branch was embolized using metal coils.
After treatment, ammonia immediately normalized (42 μg/dL) and remained without elevation thereafter.
No elevation in ammonia was observed even after discontinuation of lactitol.
[Discussion] This case involved hepatic encephalopathy that developed suddenly without underlying liver disease, but abdominal ultrasonography and contrast-enhanced CT allowed prompt diagnosis and progression to treatment.
Reported causes of hepatic encephalopathy include portosystemic shunts associated with cirrhosis or portal hypertension and congenital metabolic disorders of the urea cycle, as well as a portosystemic shunt without liver disease, as in this case. Among these, an intrahepatic portal-hepatic venous shunt is considered rare.
Regarding etiology, an acquired origin is presumed when there is a history of trauma, liver biopsy, or similar events.
This patient had no medical history other than acute myocardial infarction, and the condition was considered congenital.
There are also reports of incidental diagnosis in asymptomatic patients and of diagnosis only after hepatic encephalopathy develops in old age; thus, this condition was considered important to keep in mind in the differential diagnosis of hepatic encephalopathy in patients with noncirrhotic livers.
[Conclusion] Percutaneous transhepatic obliteration was effective for hepatic encephalopathy due to an intrahepatic portal-hepatic venous shunt.

Introduction
Among children (and adults) with extremely severe disabilities admitted for short-term stays, many exhibit physical changes such as muscle tension and epileptic seizures due to stress caused by the change in their living environment to a hospital.
We report a case in which measures to relieve tension and assistance with sputum clearance led to improved respiratory status in a mechanically ventilated child (or adult) with severe motor and intellectual disabilities who exhibited deterioration in respiratory status due to muscle tension.
Case presentation
Mr. A, a man in his 20s. Diagnoses: cerebral palsy, intellectual developmental delay. On a ventilator (Trilogy 100) 24 hours a day.
Ethical considerations
The family was informed that privacy would be protected, and consent for presentation was obtained.
Nursing care provided
Nursing problem: High risk of deterioration in respiratory status due to increased muscle tension. Nursing goal: Reduce muscle tension and minimize deterioration in respiratory status. Mr. A exhibited muscle tension manifesting as backward arching of the entire body and muscle tension manifesting as flexion of the upper limbs, decreased SpO2 and tidal volume, and increased heart rate and respiratory rate, with inadequate ventilation. His lower limbs and trunk were supported with towels to broaden the base of support and maintain limb stability.
Reassuring verbal communication and touch were also provided, his favorite music was played, and the environment was adjusted for comfort.
As a result, backward arching of the entire body disappeared, and he was observed smiling.
Next, postural drainage was performed, followed by exercises involving external rotation of the upper limbs in synchrony with inspiration and squeezing, resulting in an observed increase in SpO2.
Discussion
Managing muscle tension requires consideration of its causes and contributing factors, psychological support, and postural management.
Although verbal communication was not possible, Mr. A responded when spoken to. Providing psychological support through verbal communication and touch was reassuring for him and was effective in relieving muscle tension.
In addition, combining individualized chest expansion exercises with squeezing to facilitate expectoration of sputum and assisting respiratory movements to promote ventilation were important in improving respiratory status.
Conclusion
Abnormal muscle tension, deformities and contractures, and respiratory impairment are closely related. Investigating the causes of muscle tension and striving to eliminate them can help prevent worsening of respiratory status.

Introduction
Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a condition in which a thrombus forms through blood coagulation within deep veins such as the femoral vein and common iliac vein.
Reports of DVT in long-term bedridden children and adults with severe motor and intellectual disabilities (hereafter, severely disabled individuals) are surprisingly few. We also presented a case report at this society in 2007, but the pathophysiology remains unclear.
We report here on DVT screening performed in severely disabled individuals.
Subjects and Methods
The subjects were nine long-term residents of our center (three males and six females), all classified as Oshima classification 1.
Venous ultrasonography was performed to evaluate DVT in the deep veins of the lower extremities.
Blood coagulation tests, including D-dimer, were also performed.
Regarding ethical considerations, approval was obtained from our center's ethics committee.
Results
The subjects were 10–55 years old (median, 45 years), and asymptomatic DVT was observed in two of the nine cases (22.2%).
The site of DVT was the left common femoral vein in both cases.
The soleal veins were underdeveloped, and no thrombus at this site was observed in any case.
Blood coagulation tests showed elevated antithrombin III, FDP, and D-dimer levels in some cases, but the values were within the reference ranges in both cases with a thrombus.
Discussion
DVT in the pelvic and lower-extremity veins is classified by its site into a proximal type (iliac type and femoral type), involving the popliteal vein and veins proximal to it, and a distal type (calf type), involving veins distal to it.
DVT is usually of the distal type, and the soleal veins are considered to be the most common initial site.
However, as reported by Omori et al. (2012), these veins are underdeveloped in severely disabled individuals, who have often been bedridden since birth, and DVT at this site is uncommon.
In the present study as well, both cases of DVT were of the proximal type. In addition to motor impairment due to prolonged bed rest, mild dehydration from sweating due to increased muscle tone was also suspected as a contributing factor to thrombus formation.
A study involving a larger number of cases is currently being conducted by Omori et al.

[Objective] In patients with liver cirrhosis presenting with hematemesis and bloody stools, we often encounter cases in which no clear source of bleeding can be identified even after upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy. We report a case of a patient with liver cirrhosis who suffered death from hemorrhagic shock at our hospital, in whom pathological autopsy suggested that the cause was portal hypertensive enteropathy induced by portal vein thrombosis formation.
[Case] The patient was an 81-year-old man who had been attending our hospital for liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma since year X−5. In August of year X, he was found collapsed at home and was transported to our hospital by ambulance with the chief complaints of decreased level of consciousness and passage of bloody stools.
[Clinical Course] His level of consciousness was E4V5M6, and he had a small amount of hematemesis and a large quantity of dark red stools. Upper gastrointestinal bleeding was suspected, and endoscopy was repeated, but no clear source of bleeding could be identified. On the same day, EIS was performed in consideration of spontaneous hemostasis following rupture of esophageal varices. On hospital day 2, he had no hematemesis or bloody stools, but on hospital day 3, passage of a large quantity of tarry stools recurred, followed by respiratory arrest. Resuscitation was performed, but he did not recover, and death was confirmed.
[Discussion] At pathological autopsy, the mucosa from the lower small intestine to the large intestine was intermittently dark purple, and a large quantity of dark red bloody stools was observed within the lumen; therefore, the main lesion was considered to be lower gastrointestinal bleeding. In addition, mild vascular proliferation and dilation was observed in the submucosa of the lower gastrointestinal tract, suggesting the presence of portal hypertensive enteropathy. Furthermore, the portal vein thrombosis noted on the immediately preceding CT extended into the superior mesenteric vein, suggesting the possibility that a further rise in intravascular pressure in veins already under elevated pressure due to portal hypertensive enteropathy resulted in lower gastrointestinal bleeding from diffuse hemorrhage.
[Conclusion] Currently, portal hypertensive enteropathy has no characteristic endoscopic or pathological findings, and there are no unified diagnostic criteria or severity classifications. Thrombosis is also difficult to diagnose because its symptoms are nonspecific, and one report states that 48 hours elapsed between symptom onset and diagnosis in 75% of all cases. When patients with portal hypertension accompanied by thrombosis pass bloody stools, it is important to include massive passage of bloody stools due to diffuse bleeding from the lower gastrointestinal tract in the differential diagnosis. In patients who have developed portal hypertensive disease, it is also important to consider early the priorities and necessity of additional investigations and treatment at the time thrombosis develops.

In recent years, the usefulness of rifaximin, a poorly absorbed antibiotic, and L-carnitine preparations has also been reported.

In this case, strict fluid management was necessary during treatment for heart failure, and encephalopathy readily developed with dehydration; therefore, shunt embolization was considered indicated.

Liver biopsy shows findings resembling autoimmune hepatitis, but few reports are available.
We report a case of acute liver injury caused by Pembrolizumab.
【Case】The patient was a man in his 60s.
He was diagnosed with Stage 4 lung cancer with bone metastases in November 201x.
Because PD-L1 expression was confirmed, treatment with pembrolizumab at 200 mg every 3 weeks was initiated in December.
At cycle 4, AST was 44 IU/L and ALT was 63 IU/L.
Blood tests at the time of cycle 5 showed AST of 120 IU/L and ALT of 176 IU/L, and treatment was discontinued. However, liver dysfunction subsequently worsened, and decreased appetite was also noted, prompting hospitalization.
Height was 163 cm and weight was 66 kg. No particular abnormalities were noted on abdominal examination.
On admission, AST was 1361 IU/L, ALT 1593 IU/L, T-Bil 1.1 mg/dL, IgG 1027 mg/dl, PT 81%, M2BPGi 1.06, and ANA titer 1:40; HCV antibody and HBsAg were negative.
Ultrasound showed fatty liver, with no atrophy or ascites.
Histopathological findings included extensive hepatocyte loss, hemorrhage, and infiltration of macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells around the central veins.
Spotty necrosis was observed within the lobules, and mild lymphoplasmacytic infiltration was observed in the portal areas.
After administration of Methylprednisolone 1000 mg for 3 days, AST decreased to 270 IU/L and ALT to 822 IU/L, showing a trend toward improvement.
Thereafter, prednisolone was initiated at 1 mg/kg/day and gradually tapered, and AST/ALT returned to the reference range after approximately 2 months.
【Discussion】One characteristic of immune checkpoint inhibitors is their sustained efficacy, with antitumor effects persisting for a long time even after treatment discontinuation.
Meanwhile, irAEs are also said to persist similarly.
In hepatocellular-type drug-induced liver injury, liver injury usually often resolves promptly upon discontinuation of the causative drug, but with immune checkpoint inhibitors, some cases worsen after drug discontinuation.
In this case as well, liver enzymes rose rapidly even after drug discontinuation.
We consider it essential to perform liver biopsy early to establish the diagnosis and then promptly initiate steroid therapy.

[Introduction] Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are drugs that exert antitumor effects by inhibiting immunosuppressive pathways and activating antitumor immunity.
Since their approval for malignant melanoma in 2014, their indications have expanded to include gastric cancer and other cancers, but the frequency of immune-related adverse events (irAEs) has increased.
Liver injury as an irAE presents with various clinical manifestations, and much remains unknown.
We report a case of suspected liver injury caused by immune checkpoint inhibitors.
[Case] A woman in her 70s.
Past medical history: Hypertension and hyperlipidemia.
Alcohol history: None. History of present illness: In June 20XX-1, nivolumab, an anti-PD1 antibody, was initiated by the dermatology department at our hospital for vulvar malignant melanoma with pulmonary metastases.
The pulmonary metastatic lesions subsequently showed a tendency to shrink, and the primary vulvar lesion was resected in November 20XX-1.
Nivolumab was administered through the 15th cycle, but in January 20XX, a metastatic lesion appeared in the vulva, and the pulmonary metastatic lesions also showed a tendency to enlarge.
Ipilimumab, an anti-CTLA-4 antibody, was initiated in late February 20XX, and the second cycle was administered by mid-March.
At admission to the dermatology department in early April 20XX, she had no subjective symptoms, but blood tests revealed liver dysfunction with mildly elevated inflammatory markers: T-Bil 0.7 mg/dL, AST 6781 U/L, ALT 5381 U/L, ALP 2111 U/L, γ-GTP 481 U/L, PT 87.2%, white blood cell count 7950/μL, and CRP 3.97 mg/dL. Our department was consulted.
Tests for hepatitis viruses and autoantibodies were all negative.
Abdominal ultrasonography showed no morphological changes in the liver and no significant findings in the bile ducts.
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed no liver tumor, hepatic infarction, portal vein thrombosis, or bile duct tumor.
A liver biopsy was performed on hospital day 3 and revealed inflammatory cell infiltration predominantly composed of lymphocytes and proliferation of collagen fibers in the portal and central venous regions, but inflammatory cell infiltration into the bile duct epithelium was minimal, and no fibrous thickening of the bile ducts was observed.
The DDW-J2004 drug-induced liver injury workshop scores were 8 points for nivolumab and 9 points for ipilimumab, and these were considered suspected causative drugs for drug-induced liver injury.
Administration of PSL 45 mg/day (1 mg/kg/day) was initiated on hospital day 4.
The liver dysfunction improved, PSL was gradually tapered, and she was discharged on hospital day 49.
[Discussion] Liver failure with elevated hepatobiliary enzymes, hepatitis, and sclerosing cholangitis have been reported as forms of liver injury occurring as irAEs.
Proposed mechanisms include the unmasking of autoimmune responses by ICIs and the development of cross-reactivity between cancer cell neoantigens and self-antigens, which differ from the conventional allergic, metabolic, and other mechanisms of drug-induced liver injury. The clinical course suggested liver injury caused by ICIs, and the pathophysiology was investigated based on the histopathological findings from the liver biopsy.

[Chief complaint] Fever

[Discussion] We encountered a case of acute liver failure accompanied by marked eosinophilia.

The procedure was completed without problems, and the postoperative course was free of major complications.
The blood ammonia level normalized promptly after the procedure, and no subsequent episodes of encephalopathy have been observed.

Medical treatment includes restriction of protein intake and oral administration or intravenous infusion of lactulose or branched-chain amino acid preparations.

Although the treatment course often generally shows a marked response, cases of ascites accumulation and worsening varices have also been reported, and careful consideration is thought to be necessary when determining treatment indications.
In this case, strict fluid management was necessary during treatment for heart failure, and encephalopathy readily developed with dehydration; therefore, shunt embolization was considered indicated.

[Conclusion] We report a case in which hepatic coma was successfully controlled by embolizing a splenorenal shunt using a vascular plug.

Various hepatitis virus markers were negative; CMV- and EBV-related antigen-antibody reactions showed patterns of past infection; IgG was 1569 mg/dl, the antinuclear antibody titer was less than 1:40, and anti-M2 antibody was negative.
WBC was 4900/μl, RBC 410 × 10⁴/μl, Hb 2.1 g/dl, Ht 6.2%, MCV 151.2 fl, MCHC 51.2 Pg, and Plt 10.7 × 10⁴/μl. An increased reticulocyte count was noted, and a peripheral blood smear showed fragmented red blood cells reflecting hemolysis and spur cells (acanthocytes).
Percutaneous liver biopsy revealed hepatocyte ballooning and Mallory bodies, as well as pericellular fibrosis and inflammatory cell infiltration, leading to a diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis complicated by Spur cell anemia.
Nutritional therapy for cirrhosis and blood transfusions for anemia were provided, but lung field radiolucency gradually decreased, and poor oxygenation developed.
He was placed on mechanical ventilation and received blood transfusions, plasma filtration with dialysis, and continuous intravenous infusion of diuretics.
Multidisciplinary treatment allowed weaning from mechanical ventilation, and he has now been discharged and is receiving outpatient follow-up.
[Discussion] Spur cell anemia is a rare complication of cirrhosis first reported by Smith et al. in 1964, in which Spur cells with spiculated red blood cell morphological abnormalities appear in the peripheral blood and cause severe hemolytic changes.
Spur cell anemia has been reported as a poor prognostic factor in cirrhosis, and liver transplantation is considered the only treatment. In this case, however, multidisciplinary treatment enabled outpatient follow-up without liver transplantation.
Few reports describe alcoholic cirrhosis in young patients complicated by Spur cell anemia with a favorable clinical course; we report this case with a review of the literature.

translation.text:
We report a case of sarcoidosis with concomitant esophageal cancer.
The patient was a 69-year-old man.
He visited his previous physician with a chief complaint of a sensation of food sticking after meals, was diagnosed with esophageal cancer, and was referred to our hospital.
CT showed enlargement of the hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes, and PET-CT showed uptake in the middle thoracic esophagus and mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes.
Although the lower thoracic paraesophageal lymph nodes (110) and middle esophagus showed abnormally high uptake, the hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes showed low uptake, raising suspicion of concomitant esophageal cancer and malignant lymphoma.
A mediastinal lymph node biopsy was therefore performed and yielded a diagnosis of sarcoidosis, leading to a diagnosis of esophageal cancer with concomitant sarcoidosis.
Because lymph node metastasis was suspected, thoracoscopically assisted subtotal esophagectomy was performed after preoperative chemotherapy.
Intraoperative findings included enlarged lymph nodes in the upper and middle mediastinum. A portion was submitted for intraoperative frozen-section examination, which yielded a diagnosis of sarcoidosis; therefore, dissection of the peritracheal lymph nodes was omitted in consideration of the risk of bleeding.
The postoperative course was favorable, and the patient was discharged on hospital day 27. Histopathological findings were Mt, Type 2+0-2b, 45 × 30 mm, pT3, INFb, 1y3, v1, IM1, N1 (1/22), MO, PMO, DMO, RMO, stage 3.
Lymph node metastasis was observed only in the station 110 lymph nodes identified on preoperative PET-CT, while multiple noncaseating granulomas were observed in the other dissected lymph nodes.
At present, 4 months after surgery, no recurrence or metastasis has occurred.
In esophageal cancer with concomitant sarcoidosis, preoperative differentiation of enlarged lymph nodes is often difficult, and the extent of lymph node dissection remains controversial.
Preoperative PET-CT and intraoperative frozen-section examination were considered useful for reducing the risk of perioperative complications and determining the extent of lymph node dissection.

translation.question: What is the likelihood that "epithelioid cell nodules" are an ADE (adverse event) in the following case report?
translation.text:
A 3-year-old boy.
Initial visit: November 9, 1984.
In August 1983, he contracted varicella at the age of 2 years and 4 months.
In December of the same year, his mother noticed infiltrated dark red macules corresponding to scars throughout his body, and pain in the joints of his hands and feet reportedly also developed.
He visited another hospital, where a skin lesion was biopsied, but a definitive diagnosis was not reached.
Six months later, most of the skin lesions had faded in color and the infiltration had subsided, but in November 1984, he was admitted to the pediatric department of our hospital for further evaluation and was seen in the dermatology department.
Current findings: Numerous disseminated brownish scars measuring up to 7–8 mm in diameter were present over almost the entire body, and scattered pale reddish-brown macules with mild palpable infiltration were observed on the face and lower extremities.
Biopsy of an infiltrated reddish-brown macule revealed epithelioid cell nodules throughout the full thickness of the dermis.
Although BHL was negative, this condition was diagnosed based on elevated ACE, bilateral uveitis, posterior synechiae of the iris, joint swelling, and a negative tuberculin reaction.
Subsequently, the skin lesions resolved, but swelling of the joints of the hands and feet and elevated ACE persisted, and his current ophthalmologic status is hand-motion vision.
We report this case of the condition in a young child, characterized by specific skin lesions corresponding to post-varicella scars, joint swelling, and ocular symptoms.

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is it that the "peritoneal dissemination lesions" are an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
The patient was a 15-year-old girl.
At age 9, she underwent resection of a right ovarian immature teratoma and chemotherapy.
Subsequently, the peritoneal dissemination lesions enlarged, and resection was performed at age 10.
At age 11, she developed ileus, and laparotomy was performed because ileus symptoms accompanied by bloody stools persisted.
Marked edema was noted in portions of the small intestine, and this was not adhesive ileus.
Postoperatively, she developed marked hypoproteinemia and was diagnosed with protein-losing enteropathy.
Administration of albumin preparations and steroids was initiated.
Subsequently, her symptoms improved, but ileus symptoms recurred repeatedly.
At age 14, small intestinal stenosis was suspected, prompting repeat laparotomy. Localized stenosis was found in the middle portion of the small intestine, and that segment was resected.
Pathologically, ganglioneurosis and proliferation of the nerve plexuses were observed, and the lesion was considered attributable to abnormalities of the gastrointestinal nerves, but its underlying nature remains unclear.
Clinically, the condition was considered to be acquired chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction of unknown etiology.
After the final operation, her symptoms diminished, and steroids are being tapered.

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is it that micrognathia is an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
【Case】A 1-year-old boy
【Past medical history】Micrognathia, dysphagia, growth impairment, developmental delay, gastroesophageal reflux disease, recurrent bacterial infections
【Test results】Eosinophil count 3663/μl, IgE 1238 U/ml, RAST: milk 24.30 U/ml, soy 1.22 U/ml; stool eosinophils positive
【Clinical course】Since birth, milk had been administered through a gastric tube because of dysphagia. Intractable vomiting developed at approximately 1 year and 1 month of age.
Worsening GER was considered, and PPI and other treatments were used, but were ineffective.
Because the eosinophil count was elevated, milk allergy was considered, and switching to an extensively hydrolyzed formula resulted in improvement of symptoms.
However, because nausea persisted, the formula was changed to an amino acid formula (Elental P), after which vomiting worsened again.
Therefore, tube feeding was replaced with total parenteral nutrition.
Symptoms improved but did not resolve.
Gastric biopsy revealed eosinophilic infiltration, and eosinophilic gastroenteritis was diagnosed.
Soy protein contamination in the lipid preparation was considered the source of the causative protein, and discontinuation of this preparation resulted in resolution of symptoms.
Subsequently, tube feeding was initiated with a soy-free amino acid formula (Elemental Formula), and no recurrence of symptoms has been observed.
【Summary】We encountered a case of eosinophilic gastroenteritis thought to be caused by milk and soy.
There have been few reports of allergy due to soy protein contaminating lipid preparations, and no cases of eosinophilic gastroenteritis have been reported to date.

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is it that the "mass" is an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
The patient was a 20-year-old man.
On May 15, 2007, he presented to the emergency department with unsteadiness and gross hematuria.
Immediately before CT, he developed hemorrhagic shock and was admitted emergently.
Abdominopelvic CT revealed a mass in the bladder.
On May 16, Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated blood flow within the mass in the bladder, and MRI revealed a tumor within a hematoma, leading to a diagnosis of a bladder tumor.
Gross hematuria remained unchanged, and Ht remained in the 20% range despite blood transfusion.
On the same day, emergency angiography was performed via the femoral artery.
Two arteries branching from the left internal iliac artery and supplying the tumor in the bladder were identified, and embolization was performed using Gelfoam.
The gross hematuria became less pronounced, and TUR-Bt was performed on May 17.
A tumor measuring approximately 5 cm was identified extending from the bladder dome to the posterior wall.
The tumor was resected.
The resected specimen weighed 33 g.
Histopathological findings were TCC, G1, pTa, and the clinical stage was pTa, N0, M0.
Beginning on June 29, eight intravesical BCG instillations were administered to prevent recurrence.
No recurrence has been observed as of 1 year and 4 months after surgery.
Bladder cancer in young patients is clinically rare.
We report a case of hemorrhagic shock caused by superficial bladder cancer in a 20-year-old man, together with a brief review of the literature.

History of present illness: Abnormal liver function had been noted for 13 years, but there had been no jaundice, pruritus, or medication use.

Cell-mediated immunity is currently under investigation.

translation.question: What is the likelihood that "decompensated cirrhosis" is an ADE (adverse event) in the following case report?
translation.text:
[Background] Helicobacter cinaedi (H. cinaedi) is a Gram-negative spiral-shaped bacillus discovered in the 1980s.
It is an enterohepatic organism, and isolation of this organism from the intestinal tract, liver, and blood of patients with impaired immune function due to an underlying disease or chemotherapy has been reported.
We report a case of H. cinaedi bacteremia and cellulitis complicating decompensated cirrhosis.
[Case] A 61-year-old man with hepatitis C-related decompensated cirrhosis.
He was admitted for control of refractory hepatic ascites.
He had had brownish vomiting since the day before admission, and anemia was noted, with Hb of 7.4 g/dl; upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed for further evaluation.
The examination showed no active bleeding, but revealed LA classification Grade C reflux esophagitis, and bleeding from that site was suspected.
There was no vomiting after resumption of meals, but hypoalbuminemia progressed due to reduced food intake, and ascites worsened again.
Ascites did not improve despite combined furosemide and spironolactone, and oral tolvaptan (3.75 mg/day) was started on hospital day 7.
On hospital day 9, a fever of 38°C developed without physical symptoms.
Intermittent fever continued through hospital day 14, and pain, erythema, warmth, and swelling of both lower legs developed on hospital day 15.
MRI of the lower legs showed high signal intensity on T2WI along the fascia of both lower legs, and cellulitis was diagnosed.
To identify the causative organism, blood cultures were obtained on hospital days 11, 13, and 15, and H. cinaedi was detected in all of them.
The time to blood culture positivity was 113–150 hours.
Ceftriaxone (2 g/day), started on hospital day 15, was continued for bacteremia and cellulitis caused by this organism.
Because the symptoms improved, treatment was switched to oral minocycline (200 mg/day) on hospital day 29, and he was discharged on hospital day 36.
[Discussion] H. cinaedi infection is often detected by blood cultures obtained from patients with conditions such as cellulitis or proctitis.
However, cultures require 5–7 days, and in some cases more than 10 days, to become positive, and may not become positive within the usual incubation period; if this organism is suspected, prolonged incubation of blood cultures must be requested.
Frequent recurrence, nosocomial infection, and horizontal transmission have also been reported.
As in this case, H. cinaedi should be considered as a causative organism of infection in patients with impaired immune function, including those with decompensated cirrhosis, when undertaking further evaluation and treatment.

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is it that "acantholysis" is an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
A 65-year-old man.
In August 1985, he underwent right pneumonectomy for squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.
In November of the same year, pruritic erythema, blisters, and erosions appeared on the anterior chest and improved with topical betamethasone valerate ointment.

The skin lesions have improved with topical therapy alone.

translation.question: What is the likelihood that the "stenotic findings" in the following case report represent an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
Case: A 66-year-old woman
History of present illness: She underwent total gastrectomy (D2) for gastric cancer and resection of bilateral ovarian tumors (dermoid cyst).
The pathological findings were 55 x 50 mm, Type 3 poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma, si (panc. capsule), ly2, v2, n2 (12/76), stage 3b. Intraoperative ascitic fluid cytology was Class 1.

[At 1 year and 6 months postoperatively: CEA (10.3), CA19-9 (0.6 or less)] At 1 year and 7 months postoperatively, she was admitted with complaints of abdominal pain and vomiting.
Blood test findings on admission: CRP 0.0 mg/dl, WBC 5400, Hb 12.7 g/dl, Plt 285,000, CEA 11.1 ng/ml. Imaging findings: CT showed rectal wall thickening, and a contrast enema showed stenotic findings in the rectum.

It was considered necessary to follow patients with Se or deeper invasion with rectal metastasis in mind when no recurrent lesion can be identified.

translation.text:
Case: A 48-year-old woman.
Chief complaint: Multiple skin tumors.
Family history: Mother: malignant lymphoma; eldest son: autism.
History of present illness: Onset around 1965. Tumor stage since around 1984.
She had received PUVA therapy, topical ACNU lotion, local IFN-α injections, cobalt irradiation, and other treatments at Juntendo University Hospital.
She was subsequently transferred to our hospital for electron beam irradiation.
From 1988, she was treated with VEPA therapy, electron beam irradiation, systemic IFN-α administration, and other treatments.
During the course, an elevated ATL antibody titer was observed, so testing for HTLV-1 proviral DNA was performed.
Blood tests were positive for HTLV-I provirus, showed an ATL antibody titer of at least 1:256, were negative for T-cell receptor β-chain rearrangement (Tcβ), and showed an elevated IL-2 receptor level; she was therefore diagnosed as an HTLV-1 carrier.
In contrast, the tumor was positive for both HTLV-I provirus and T-cell receptor β-chain rearrangement (Tcβ).
Systemic IFN-α administration was effective as treatment, and survival for six years in the tumor stage was considered relatively long-term survival.

translation.text:
Delayed wound healing due to inhibition of angiogenesis has been reported as an adverse event of Bevacizumab. We report a case in which emergency bowel resection and anastomosis were performed during bevacizumab treatment, with a favorable course without complications such as anastomotic leakage, together with a brief review of the literature.
The patient was a 68-year-old man.
In November 2011, right hemicolectomy and D2 lymph node dissection were performed for ascending colon cancer with multiple liver and lung metastases.
The postoperative diagnosis was CK(A), Type 2, 55 × 40 mm, tub2, pSI, N3, H3, P0, M1 (LM3), fStage IV, and XELOX + bevacizumab was started on postoperative day 17.
On day 20 after the start of cycle 13 (oxaliplatin had been withheld since cycle 10, and bevacizumab had been administered 12 times), he presented to a local physician with chief complaints of abdominal pain and vomiting and was transferred to our hospital with a diagnosis of bowel obstruction.
Abdominal contrast-enhanced CT showed localized small bowel dilatation, poor enhancement of the bowel wall, and a closed loop. Strangulated bowel obstruction was diagnosed, and emergency surgery was performed the same day.
Operative findings revealed necrosis of approximately 60 cm of the ileum due to strangulation by a band.
The necrotic bowel was resected, an end-to-side anastomosis was performed using a circular stapler (28 mm), and the blind end was closed using a linear stapler.
The postoperative course was uneventful without complications other than a perianal abscess that developed on postoperative day 5.
Oral feeding was started on postoperative day 7, and after oral Xeloda was started on postoperative day 14, he improved and was discharged.

translation.text:

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is "right pleural effusion" to be an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
Pulmonary torsion is a complication of lung resection, but it has also occurred extremely rarely after esophagectomy.
We report a case of right middle lobe torsion following surgery for esophageal cancer.
The patient was a 68-year-old man.
For thoracic esophageal cancer, cT2N0M0 stage II, he underwent subtotal esophagectomy via right thoracotomy, two-field lymph node dissection, and gastric conduit reconstruction via the posterior mediastinal route with cervical anastomosis after preoperative chemotherapy (2 courses of FP).
The operative time was 10 hours 2 minutes, blood loss was 305 ml, and the thoracic portion of the procedure lasted 4 hours 39 minutes.
On postoperative day 9, he developed a fever of 37.7°C, and contrast-enhanced chest CT showed a right intrathoracic hematoma, bilateral pneumonia, and right middle lobe atelectasis. Antibiotic therapy and intensified physiotherapy were instituted.
Subsequently, worsening right pleural effusion was noted on chest radiography. Repeat contrast-enhanced chest CT on postoperative day 16 revealed a new thrombus in the right lower lobe pulmonary artery, with no improvement in the right middle lobe atelectasis.
Bronchoscopy revealed narrowing of the right middle lobe bronchial lumen and twisting of the right upper lobe bronchus.
Although manual air insufflation produced slight improvement in the right middle lobe atelectasis, the bronchial twisting did not improve.
Based on these findings, right middle lobe torsion was diagnosed, and emergency surgery was performed after IVC filter placement.
An anterolateral thoracotomy was performed through the right fourth intercostal space. Adhesions to the chest wall, predominantly involving the right upper lobe, were present and were dissected.
When the adhesions between the lung and the mediastinal pleura were dissected while taking care to avoid gastric conduit injury, the middle lobe was found extending cranially along the mediastinal side of the upper lobe.
As interlobar dissection proceeded, adhesions were found between the ventral aspect of middle lobe S5 and the cranial aspect of lower lobe S6, and the middle lobe was twisted approximately 90 degrees counterclockwise.
Division of these adhesions released the middle lobe torsion.
The patient was observed for approximately 15 minutes with bilateral lung ventilation. There was no abnormal lung discoloration, no changes in vital signs, and no development of acidosis, so lung resection was deemed unnecessary.
Because this was not a post-lung-resection case, interlobar fixation was also deemed unnecessary.
The course after reoperation was generally favorable.

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is it that "erythema with scaling" is an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
Psoriasis vulgaris is an inflammatory keratinization disorder thought to develop when environmental factors such as stress, alcohol consumption, and smoking act on a genetic predisposition, but its association with colorectal cancer is unknown.
We report a case of synchronous multiple colorectal cancers arising in the cecum and sigmoid colon during treatment for psoriasis vulgaris.
[Case] A 60-year-old man.
[Chief complaint] Positive fecal occult blood test.
[History of present illness] The patient had had psoriasis vulgaris for 5 years and had been receiving treatment with topical steroids and adalimumab in the dermatology department of our hospital.
In September 2012, a positive fecal occult blood test prompted further investigation.
Colonoscopy revealed a type 0-IIa lesion in the cecum and a type 1 lesion in the sigmoid colon, and he was referred to the surgery department for surgery.
[Past medical history] Hypertension and hyperuricemia.
[Physical findings on admission] Height 159.5 cm, weight 66.1 kg, temperature 35.6°C, blood pressure 149/99 mmHg, and pulse 68 beats/min.
The abdomen was flat and soft, with no tenderness.
Erythema with scaling was observed predominantly on the face and trunk.
[Treatment course] Laparoscopy-assisted ileocecal resection and sigmoid colectomy were performed in January 2013.
The operation was performed using 5 ports, and reconstruction was performed with end-to-end anastomoses using FEEA and DST, respectively.
The operative time was 5 hours 49 minutes, and blood loss was 40 mL.
He was discharged on postoperative day 9.
No change in the skin lesions was observed postoperatively.
[Histopathological examination] The findings were C, type 0-IIa, pM, tub1 in adenoma, pN0, sH0, sP0, M0, fStage 0; and S, type 1, tub1, pSS, sN0, sP0, cM0, fStage II.

translation.text:
A 56-year-old woman.
First seen on March 28, 1990.
Around October 1985, a heat rash-like eruption appeared over the pretibial areas.
Around June of the following year, it subsided, leaving pigmentation.
Thereafter, the eruption appeared and worsened every winter.
In 1988, an eruption also appeared on the face.
Around autumn 1989, topical and oral steroids were administered, but the eruption worsened when the dose was reduced, prompting her initial visit to our department.
At the initial visit, erythematous lesions measuring 2–5 cm in diameter with palpable infiltration were scattered or clustered and coalescent, predominantly on the face and back.
Mildly atrophic scars and pigmentation were also scattered.
Histology of the erythema on the back showed dense neutrophilic infiltration from the upper to lower dermis and abundant nuclear debris, with no evidence of vasculitis.
Direct immunofluorescence was negative.

[Chief complaint] Impaired consciousness.
[Past medical history] Esophageal varices.

On this occasion, she again developed impaired consciousness and presented to the emergency department.

Blood biochemical tests showed Alb 3.0 g/dL, T.Bil 1.1 mg/dL, NH3 138 μg/dL, PLT 11.8 × 10^4/μL, PT 63.6%, and PT-INR 1.30.
Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a large splenorenal shunt.
Her consciousness improved to grade I hepatic coma with intravenous infusion of BCAA preparations.
Splenorenal shunt occlusion was performed after thorough IC with the family.
The splenorenal shunt was embolized with an AMPLATZER™ Vascular Plug via a right femoral venous approach.
No particular intraoperative complications were observed.

Embolization using a vascular plug was considered to allow safe treatment without these risks.
[Conclusion] We report a case in which hepatic coma was successfully controlled by embolizing a splenorenal shunt using a vascular plug.

translation.text:
[Introduction] In recent years, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) have been indicated for various malignancies, and their efficacy has been demonstrated.

There have also been reports that MMF is effective in steroid-resistant cases, and it was introduced in this case as well, but its efficacy could not be evaluated.
The number of cases of liver injury due to irAE is expected to increase in the future, and accumulation of cases and consideration of early immunosuppressive therapy are thought to be necessary.

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is "diffuse dilatation and wall thickening" to be an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
The patient was a man in his 60s who was receiving Nivolumab 150 mg every 2 weeks as second-line treatment for laryngeal cancer in the Department of Otolaryngology at our hospital.
Blood tests 4 months after treatment initiation showed T-bil 0.81 mg/dl, AST 91 U/l, ALT 144 U/l, ALP 1478 U/l, and γGT 426 U/l, indicating liver injury with predominant elevation of biliary enzymes, and he was referred to the Department of Gastroenterology.
He had no subjective symptoms other than a fever of 37.6°C, and abdominal examination revealed no remarkable findings.
Blood biochemical testing was negative for various viral markers, ANA, and AMA2, and IgG and IgG4 were within normal limits.
CT showed diffuse dilatation and wall thickening of the common bile duct and the right and left hepatic ducts, as well as gallbladder enlargement and gallbladder wall thickening, but MRCP and ERC showed no strictures or neoplastic lesions in the bile ducts.
Liver histology showed no prominent inflammatory changes or necrosis of hepatocytes, but revealed infiltration by diverse inflammatory cells in the portal areas and focal features of nonsuppurative destructive cholangitis.
Based on these findings, immune checkpoint inhibitor-related cholangitis was suspected, and Nivolumab was discontinued. However, there was no improvement in biochemical or imaging findings, so PSL 30 mg was started.
Hepatobiliary enzyme levels gradually improved, but cholangitis worsened again when PSL was tapered to 15 mg, so UDCA 600 mg was added.
Cholangitis subsequently improved, and PSL was discontinued, leaving UDCA monotherapy.
A response had been achieved with Nivolumab, but the tumor progressed again after treatment was suspended. Systemic chemotherapy with cytotoxic anticancer agents was administered but was ineffective. Because no recurrence of cholangitis was observed during that period, and in view of the patient's strong wishes, Nivolumab was resumed following discussion.
More than 8 months have since elapsed without recurrent liver dysfunction, and the tumor has begun to shrink again.
Cholangitis is rarely reported as an immune checkpoint inhibitor-related adverse event (irAE), and there is currently no consensus regarding its treatment.
It also remains unclear whether anti-PD-1 antibodies should be readministered or permanently discontinued after recovery from irAEs, including cholangitis.
We report this rare case, with a review of the literature, in which cholangitis improved with combined PSL and UDCA treatment and an anti-PD-1 antibody was readministered during UDCA monotherapy.

translation.question: What is the likelihood that "hepatic dysfunction" is an ADE (adverse event) in the following case report?
translation.text:
The patient was a 6-month-old girl.
She had been diagnosed prenatally with duodenal atresia.
After birth, she was also diagnosed with a high imperforate anus with a rectovaginal fistula, intestinal malrotation, and a ventricular septal defect, and underwent definitive repair of duodenal atresia and colostomy creation on day 2 of life.
Subsequently, poor weight gain attributable to the ventricular septal defect was noted, and definitive repair was performed at 5 months of age.
Gradual weight gain was noted, but she was readmitted at 6 months of age with abdominal distension and vomiting.
She was diagnosed with postoperative adhesive intestinal obstruction, and her symptoms improved with nothing by mouth and gastric decompression via a nasogastric tube.
Daikenchuto was started at 0.45 g/kg/day, also with the aim of preventing recurrence of intestinal obstruction, but abnormal liver function was noted 1 week after initiation, with GOT 105 IU/l and GPT 110 IU/l.
Viral infection and liver injury caused by other drugs were considered unlikely, so only Daikenchuto was discontinued; the values returned to nearly normal within 1 week, and no abnormal liver function has been observed since.
Hepatic dysfunction due to Daikenchuto is rare, and although it is a frequently used drug in general practice, caution was considered necessary when administering it to infants and young children.

translation.question: What is the likelihood that "diffuse erythema" is an ADE (adverse event) in the following case report?
translation.text:
A 28-year-old man.
Erythema and nail deformities had been present on the fingers since age 2, and erythema, scaling, and pustules had appeared on the trunk and extremities since age 7.
Fever occurred during exacerbations of the skin lesions.
The condition was refractory, with repeated remissions and exacerbations, but treatment with etretinate 30 mg/day was started in September 1987, and the skin lesions stabilized.
Because of elevated intraocular pressure due to glaucoma, oral acetazolamide (Diamox®) 750 mg/day was started on November 11, 1988.
From November 19 of the same year, multiple areas of erythema and numerous pustules appeared on the trunk and extremities, accompanied by fever.
After acetazolamide was discontinued, the skin lesions subsided.
The drug lymphocyte stimulation test and patch test were both negative.
Oral challenge test: Three hours after administration of acetazolamide 250 mg, diffuse erythema appeared on the trunk and extremities.
Administration was continued, and after 36 hours (total dose 1500 mg), psoriasis-like erythema, scaling, and pustules appeared.
Biopsy of the induced skin lesions revealed Munro microabscesses and Kogoj spongiform pustules.
Although several drugs are known to induce or exacerbate psoriasis, no cases of pustular psoriasis exacerbated by acetazolamide have been observed, prompting this report.

translation.question: What is the likelihood that "aspirin-induced asthma" is an ADE (adverse event) in the following case report?
translation.text:
Case: A 48-year-old male.
He had steroid-dependent bronchial asthma with onset at age 41 and a history of a severe attack induced by an analgesic in March 1986 (aspirin-induced asthma).
He began attending our outpatient department in June of the same year.
In July 1989, anterior chest pain (hereafter ACP) developed after early-morning wheezing; angina pectoris was suspected because nitroglycerin was effective.
Subsequently, chest pain almost completely disappeared with continued diltiazem use, although ACP occurred 2–3 times a year and resolved readily with oral nitroglycerin.
BD inhalation therapy was started in June 1990 and continued, but ACP recurred in late November 1992.
On December 7, he visited the outpatient department for an early-morning asthma attack. After returning home, he developed severe ACP and returned to the outpatient department by ambulance.
Chest pain had almost completely resolved on arrival, but he was admitted that day because of bradycardia.
Although PaO2 was 77 Torr on admission, wheezing gradually intensified and improved with intravenous infusion of a bronchodilator and hydrocortisone.
At 9:30 AM on December 8, ACP recurred, and EKG showed ST elevation (II, III, aVF) and ST depression (V1–5).
Emergency cardiac catheterization was performed for suspected acute myocardial infarction, but no abnormalities were found, and coronary vasospastic angina was diagnosed.
On December 9, similar chest pain developed, and intravenous heparin was effective.
Subsequently, he progressed well with continuous infusions of heparin, nitrates, and PSL and was discharged on December 29.
These findings suggest that asthma attacks contributed to coronary vasospasm in this case.

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is it that "lymphocytic infiltration and bile duct epithelial injury" represents an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
[Background] Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) have become available for various diseases, and reports of immune-related adverse events (irAE), their characteristic adverse events, are increasing. AIH-like histopathological findings have been reported in liver-related irAE, but reports of cholangitis have also appeared sporadically in recent years. We report a case of nivolumab-associated cholangitis with diverse histopathological features.
[Case] A 64-year-old man underwent distal gastrectomy for gastric cancer 1 year earlier. Following postoperative recurrence in the peritoneum and left supraclavicular lymph nodes, nivolumab was administered as 3rd line chemotherapy. After completion of 3 courses of nivolumab, a psoriasiform drug eruption appeared, accompanied by elevated hepatobiliary enzymes: AST 93 U/L, ALT 94 U/L, ALP 1341 U/L, and γGTP 149 U/L. Hepatitis virus markers were negative; the antinuclear antibody titer was 1:80, antimitochondrial antibodies were negative, IgG was 1645.6 mg/dL, IgG4 was 20.5 mg/dL, and IgM was 45.1 mg/dL. CT and MRCP showed no dilatation of the common bile duct or intrahepatic bile ducts. An irAE was suspected, and a liver biopsy was performed. Histopathological examination showed moderate inflammatory cell infiltration and endotheliitis in the portal tracts, with lymphocytic infiltration into the bile duct epithelium and bile duct epithelial injury. Noncaseating epithelioid cell granulomas containing Langhans-type multinucleated giant cells were also observed within the lobules. The lymphocytes in the portal tracts were CD8-positive and CD4-positive lymphocytes, and nivolumab-associated cholangitis was diagnosed. PSL 0.5 mg/kg was administered, and after 3 weeks, the values improved to AST 11 U/L, ALT 26 U/L, ALP 566 U/L, and γGTP 73 U/L. However, a flare occurred 2 weeks after reducing PSL to 0.4 mg/kg, and after 4 weeks, the values worsened to AST 100 U/L, ALT 104 U/L, ALP 1215 U/L, and γGTP 328 U/L, prompting another liver biopsy. Histopathological examination of the second liver biopsy showed moderate inflammatory cell infiltration in the portal tracts, with a small number of plasma cells. Interface hepatitis, lymphocytic infiltration into the bile duct epithelium, and intralobular lymphocyte aggregates were also observed. As in the first biopsy, the infiltrating lymphocytes were CD8-positive and CD4-positive lymphocytes. After increasing PSL to 1 mg/kg, hepatobiliary enzyme levels decreased, and no flare has been observed even after reducing PSL to 0.2 mg/kg.
[Discussion] ICI-associated liver injury exhibits diverse histological features. In this case, the first liver biopsy showed granuloma formation, with features resembling primary biliary cholangitis. The second liver biopsy showed AIH-like findings, including plasma cell infiltration and interface hepatitis, suggesting that ICI-associated liver injury has diverse pathogenic mechanisms.

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is it that "elevated liver enzymes" is an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
[Objective] Immune checkpoint inhibitors exert antitumor effects by inhibiting the immune system.
However, they are known to cause immune-related adverse effects (immune related Adverse Effects: irAEs) in various organs, and fatal cases have also been reported.
Liver injury is a common irAE, and according to the package insert, liver injury and hepatitis occur in approximately 10% of patients combined.
Liver biopsy shows findings resembling autoimmune hepatitis, but few reports are available.
We report a case of acute liver injury caused by Pembrolizumab.
[Case] The patient was a man in his 60s.
In November 201x, he was diagnosed with Stage 4 lung cancer with bone metastases.
Because PD-L1 expression was confirmed, pembrolizumab was initiated in December at a dose of 200 mg every 3 weeks.
At cycle 4, AST was 44 IU/L and ALT was 63 IU/L.
Blood testing at the time of cycle 5 showed AST of 120 IU/L and ALT of 176 IU/L, and treatment was discontinued. However, liver dysfunction subsequently continued to worsen, and decreased appetite was also noted, prompting hospitalization.
Height was 163 cm and weight was 66 kg. No particular abnormalities were noted on abdominal examination.
On admission, AST was 1361 IU/L, ALT 1593 IU/L, T-Bil 1.1 mg/dL, IgG 1027 mg/dl, PT 81%, M2BPGi 1.06, and ANA titer 1:40; HCV antibody and HBsAg were negative.
Ultrasonography showed no fatty liver, atrophy, or ascites.
Histopathological findings included extensive hepatocyte loss, hemorrhage, and infiltration by macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells around the central veins.
Spotty necrosis was observed within the lobules, and mild lymphoplasmacytic infiltration was observed in the portal tracts.
After administration of Methylprednisolone 1000 mg for 3 days, AST and ALT showed an improving trend, reaching 270 IU/L and 822 IU/L, respectively.
Subsequently, prednisolone was initiated at 1 mg/kg/day and gradually tapered, and AST/ALT returned to the reference range after approximately 2 months.
[Discussion] One characteristic of immune checkpoint inhibitors is their sustained efficacy, with antitumor effects persisting for a long time after treatment discontinuation.
Meanwhile, irAEs are also said to persist similarly.
Hepatocellular-type drug-induced liver injury usually often resolves rapidly after discontinuation of the causative drug, but some cases involving immune checkpoint inhibitors worsen after drug discontinuation.
In this case as well, elevated liver enzymes progressed rapidly even after drug discontinuation.
We consider it essential to perform an early liver biopsy to establish the diagnosis and then promptly initiate corticosteroids.

translation.question: How likely is it that "hepatic dysfunction" is an ADE (adverse event) in the following case report?
translation.text:
A 47-year-old woman.
Oral Salazovirin was started on May 17, 1990, for suspected ulcerative colitis. In early June, generalized malaise, fever, and low back pain developed, and Minalfen was added on June 8. On June 12, edematous erythema appeared on the face and spread over the entire body within 2–3 days, becoming associated with tense bullae on the extremities. She was admitted on June 18. High fever, lymphadenopathy, leukocytosis, and hepatic dysfunction, including GOT 147 and LDH 1028, were noted, and treatment with Predonine 60 mg was started.
The skin eruption largely resolved after approximately 2 weeks, but the white blood cell count increased to approximately 40,000, and the appearance of lymphocytes with nuclear abnormalities (maximum 16%) and elevated LDH persisted until late July.
Skin biopsy showed features of erythema multiforme with infiltration by numerous atypical lymphocytes, and lymph node biopsy also showed findings suggestive of malignant lymphoma.
Infectious mononucleosis-type drug eruption has been reported with Salazopyrin, and an oral challenge test with this drug yielded positive findings.

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is it that "organ injury" is an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
[Case] A 52-year-old man
<Chief complaints> Fever and rash
<History of present illness> Diagnosed with depression in January 2001.
May 2: Started taking amoxapine, carbamazepine, and flunitrazepam.
May 24: Developed fever (38°C) and a skin rash.
June 4: Admitted to the dermatology department of our hospital.
June 17: Developed dyspnea and was transferred to the respiratory medicine department.
<Physical findings> BH 170 cm, BW 84 kg, BT 38.5°C, BP 124/74 mmHg, PR 102/min. Palpable cervical lymph nodes (several, each approximately the size of a thumb tip). Dry rales audible during both inspiration and expiration. Generalized desquamative erythema with a tendency to coalesce.
<Complete blood count> WBC 21400/μl (St 1, Sg 23, E 7, M 6, L 57, A-L 6%), Hb 16.9 g/dl, Plt 152000.
<Serology> CRP 6.4. [Measles] IgM 0.15 (−), IgG 30.8 (+); [HHV-6] IgM <10, IgG ×20; [CMV] IgM 0.26 (−), IgG 7.4 (+); [EBV] VCA IgM <10, EBNA <10.
<Biochemistry> GOT 1911 U/L, GPT 2481 U/L, LDH 16581 U/L, γGTP 1801 U/L.
<ABG> pH 7.4, PaO2 57.0, PaCO2 36.1.
<FV curve> Low V25 (suspected peripheral airway impairment).
<Chest CT scan> Findings suggestive of thickening of the bronchiolar walls.
[Characteristics of this case]
<Clinical findings> Severe drug eruption accompanied by fever and lymphadenopathy.
<Laboratory findings and diagnostic basis> Leukocytosis, appearance of atypical lymphocytes, elevated HHV-6 IgG, elevated HHV-7 IgG, and positive DLST (carbamazepine). Based on these findings, Hypersensitivity Syndrome (HS) was diagnosed.
<Course after initiation of treatment> A rapid reduction in PSL dosage resulted in a transient relapse.
<Peripheral airway impairment> The arterial blood gas findings, chest CT scan, and pulmonary function suggested that peripheral airway impairment was present; the peripheral airway impairment resolved as treatment took effect.
[Hypersensitivity syndrome and organ injury]
<Mechanism of action> Organ injury is considered to be tissue injury caused by (CTL) as part of an immune response to eliminate virus-infected cells.
<Supporting evidence>
1. HHV-6 DNA has been detected in tissue from the lesions.
2. Relapse occurs during rapid steroid tapering.
[Conclusions]
1) HS developed during carbamazepine administration.
2) Relapse occurred during steroid tapering.
3) Bronchiolitis was observed during the clinical course but resolved as HS improved.
4) HS is often accompanied by injury to multiple organs, including the liver. Cases accompanied by bronchiolar injury are rare, but cases with lymphadenopathy alone, without skin symptoms, have also been reported; thus, it is a disease involving diverse systemic organ injury.

translation.question: What is the likelihood that "hepatocellular necrosis" is an ADE (adverse event) in the following case report?
translation.text:
The patient was a 74-year-old woman.
She was receiving outpatient treatment at the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology of our hospital for pulmonary and splenic metastases of uterine leiomyosarcoma.
Oral pazopanib 800 mg was started on December 19, 201X. However, blood tests on January 22, 201X+1 showed marked liver enzyme elevations of a mixed pattern, with T-Bil 7.85 mg/dl, D-Bil 5.07 mg/dl, AST 559 IU/L, ALT 515 IU/L, LDH 747 IU/L, and ALP 1490 IU/L, prompting consultation with our department.
Various autoantibodies and viral markers were negative.
DLST for pazopanib was negative.
Scoring using the DDW-J 2004 drug-induced liver injury workshop criteria yielded +2 for the number of days from onset, +2 for the presence or absence of causes other than drugs, and +1 for previous reports of liver injury, for a total score of 5. Drug-induced liver injury due to pazopanib was suspected, and the plan was to discontinue the drug and monitor the patient.
However, blood tests one week later showed a trend toward worsening liver function with a cholestatic pattern, with T-Bil 22.37 mg/dl, D-Bil 15.02 mg/dl, AST 447 IU/L, ALT 348 IU/L, LDH 499 IU/L, and ALP 2360 IU/L. A liver biopsy was therefore performed that day to investigate the cause.
Liver histology revealed cholestasis in hepatocytes around the central veins, inflammatory cell infiltration predominantly consisting of small lymphocytes in the Glisson's sheaths, and focal hepatocellular necrosis within the lobules. Drug-induced liver injury exhibiting impaired bile transport and features of hepatitis was diagnosed.
Although the possibility of tumor progression was also considered, liver dysfunction was the predominant pathology, and steroid pulse therapy (500 mg/day) was started that day.
One week later, hepatobiliary enzyme levels showed a tendency toward improvement, so the steroid dose was gradually tapered. Hepatobiliary enzyme levels normalized two months after treatment initiation.
Although there have been scattered reports of drug-induced liver injury due to pazopanib in Japan, few reports describe Grade 4 injury in which a liver biopsy was performed and a definitive diagnosis was established, as in this case.
We report a case of drug-induced liver injury due to pazopanib that responded to steroid pulse therapy, incorporating our experience with this case.

translation.question: How likely is it that "telangiectasia" is an ADE (adverse event) in the following case report?
translation.text:
A 41-year-old woman.
No notable past medical history.
Initial consultation: August 2, 1989.
She was admitted to the otolaryngology department for facial nerve palsy and had been receiving intravenous infusions of methylprednisolone sodium succinate (tapered from 240 mg/day) and other medications since July 21.
On August 1, pruritic erythema appeared on the neck to the anterior chest and spread, prompting referral to our department on August 2.
At the initial consultation, multiple mildly infiltrated, pruritic erythematous lesions up to the size of a fingernail were present over almost the entire body, predominantly on the face, neck, and anterior chest, with areas of coalescence also observed.
Routine blood tests and urinalysis showed no abnormalities.
Histopathological examination of the skin revealed mild telangiectasia in the superficial dermis and moderate perivascular lymphocytic infiltration.
All medications administered by the otolaryngology department were discontinued on August 2, and the erythema improved in approximately 10 days.
After the skin eruption improved, patch testing, intradermal testing, and a drug-induced lymphocyte stimulation test with methylprednisolone sodium succinate were performed, all of which were negative.
Rechallenge by intravenous infusion reproduced a similar skin eruption.
