translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is it that the "pale pink papules accompanied by intense pruritus" represent an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
Patient: A 32-year-old man.
He had been working in termite extermination for 3 years.
Initial consultation: Approximately 2 months earlier, numerous pale pink papules accompanied by intense pruritus appeared on the forearms, backs of the hands, and other areas. He was treated for dermatitis by a local physician, but there was no improvement, and he visited our department.
Skin findings at the initial consultation: Numerous discrete, millet-sized, pale pink to pale reddish-brown papules on sun-exposed areas, including the nape, forearms, and backs of the hands.
Based on the history and current findings, contact dermatitis or photocontact dermatitis due to the termite control agent used at work was suspected, and testing was performed.
The MED on the back was normal.
Patch testing with chlorpyrifos diluted 40-fold was negative to weakly positive.
Photopatch testing with the same agent (UVA 8.4 J/c, below the MED) was strongly positive, and testing at a 400-fold dilution was weakly positive.
Histological findings of the skin eruption on the back were mild spongiosis and intraepidermal cellular infiltration, with perivascular infiltration of small round cells in the upper dermis.
Chlorpyrifos is an organophosphate insecticide developed in the United States in the 1960s. It is widely used for termite control and pest extermination and is considered to have a high level of safety.
However, we encountered a case of contact dermatitis and photoallergic contact dermatitis caused by this agent.
In the future, it is desirable that sufficient attention be paid not only to liver injury but also to skin disorders in users of this agent.

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is it that antibiotics are causing an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
Case: An 81-year-old woman.
Initial visit: July 2, 1990.
She had a history of cerebral infarction and was receiving outpatient internal medicine care for hypertension and mild diabetes mellitus.
Without prodromal symptoms, multiple infiltrated erythematous lesions suddenly appeared on the trunk and extremities along with fever. From the following day, decreased consciousness was observed, and pustules appeared on the erythematous lesions and rapidly increased in number.
Histopathological examination revealed abscesses of various sizes composed of neutrophils within the stratum corneum and formation of Kogoj’s spongiform pustules in the epidermis.
Routine laboratory tests showed leukocytosis, strongly positive CRP, an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hypoproteinemia, and hypocalcemia.
Bacterial cultures of blood and pustules were negative.
There was no response to antibiotics; with administration of Tigason, the pustules rapidly disappeared, and the erythematous lesions also gradually disappeared.
Blood cytokine levels were also measured in this patient and four other patients with generalized pustular disease who had followed a similarly rapid course.
Bacterial cultures of blood and pustules were negative.
There was no response to antibiotics; with administration of Tigason, the pustules rapidly disappeared, and the erythematous lesions also gradually disappeared.
Blood cytokine levels were also measured in this patient and four other patients with generalized pustular disease who had followed a similarly rapid course.
options: Unlikely to be causing an ADE

translation.question: What is the likelihood that Obisot is causing an ADE (adverse event) in the following case report?
translation.text:
[Objective] To establish the diagnosis and investigate the mechanism of onset and treatment methods in a patient with recurrent wheals corresponding to the areas immersed during bathing.
[Methods] The patient was a 74-year-old man.
For the past 5 years, he had noticed wheals corresponding to the areas immersed during bathing and the areas in contact with a heated toilet seat. In addition to blood tests, intradermal tests with Obisot, noradrenaline, and autologous serum at room temperature and autologous serum returned to room temperature after heating, an ice cube test, and a heat provocation test were performed.
[Results] Peripheral blood findings, biochemical tests, immunoglobulins, and serum complement levels were within reference ranges, and autoantibodies were negative.
Serum total IgE was 88.41 U/ml, and specific IgE was positive only for Anisakis, at class 2.
In the heat provocation test, a beaker heated to 45°C was held against the skin for 5 minutes, and wheals were observed confined to the contact area.
Furthermore, no wheals appeared with water at 38°C; wheals appeared after 5 minutes with water at 40°C and immediately with water at 42°C.
[Conclusion] Cholinergic urticaria was ruled out because no wheals appeared with exercise-induced sweating and the intradermal test with Obisot was negative. Adrenergic urticaria was ruled out because the intradermal test with noradrenaline was negative.
Aquagenic urticaria was ruled out by a negative warm-water immersion test at 38°C, cold urticaria was ruled out by a negative ice cube test, and heat urticaria was diagnosed based on a positive heat provocation test.
In addition, intradermal tests were performed with unheated autologous serum and autologous serum heated at 42°C for 15 minutes or at 60°C for 15 minutes, both immediately after returning to room temperature and after storage at room temperature for 4 hours following heating; all were negative.
options: Unlikely to be causing an ADE

translation.question: How likely is it that fluticasone is causing an ADE (adverse event) in the following case report?
translation.text:
The mechanism of exercise-induced airway narrowing complicating cholinergic urticaria and effective medications remain unclear.
Medications to alleviate exercise-induced airway narrowing were evaluated in one girl with cholinergic urticaria.
[Case] A 12-year-old girl.
The chief complaint was itchy wheals during exercise that did not improve with oral antihistamines.
There was no history of allergic diseases such as bronchial asthma.
Cholinergic urticaria was diagnosed based on exercise-induced prurigo and a positive intradermal acetylcholine test.
The autologous serum intradermal test was negative.
IgE-RIST was 5171 U/ml, and RAST was positive for mites and HD.
[Methods] Exercise challenge tests were performed five times under identical challenge conditions: (1) before treatment, (2) after 1 month of oral epinastine + montelukast, (3) after 2 months of (2) + fluticasone 200 μg/day, (4) after (3) + repeated SABA inhalation, and (5) after (3) + repeated anticholinergic inhalation. The percentage decrease in forced expiratory volume in 1 second (ΔFEV1) and pre-challenge FeNO (ppb), measured with NIOX MINO, were evaluated.
[Results] In (1), ΔFEV1 was 19% and FeNO was 38; in (2), ΔFEV1 was 12% and FeNO was 35; in (3), ΔFEV1 was 10% and FeNO was 30; in (4), ΔFEV1 was 7% and FeNO was 35; and in (5), ΔFEV1 was 1% and FeNO was 34.
[Conclusion] ICS did not produce significant improvements in ΔFEV1 or FeNO for exercise-induced airway narrowing in this case, and antihistamines, anti-LT agents, and inhaled anticholinergics were presumed to be effective.
Neurogenic inflammation rather than eosinophilic airway inflammation was presumed to be the mechanism of exercise-induced airway narrowing.
options: Unlikely to be causing an ADE

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is it that Minomycin is causing an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
Patient: A 72-year-old woman, farmer.
First visit: January 20, 1990.
Chief complaint: Red papules on the face.
Family history: Unremarkable.
Past medical history: Ovarian cyst approximately 50 years ago; no history of tuberculosis.
History of present illness: In June 1989, a few red papules developed in both orbital regions.
Because she had no subjective symptoms, she left them untreated; the red papules in these regions increased in number, and similar papules also developed on both upper cheeks.
A short course of topical steroid ointment had been tried, but it was ineffective.
Findings at the first visit: Numerous red papules ranging from pinhead to rice-grain size were observed on the upper and lower eyelids bilaterally and on both upper cheeks.
Some papules had a yellowish hue, and some showed a tendency to coalesce.
Tuberculin reaction: Equivocal positive.
Histopathology: Nodules with central caseous necrosis surrounded by epithelioid cells and lymphocytes were observed in the dermis.
Treatment and course: Improvement occurred with oral Minomycin (200 mg/day).
Characteristics of the case: This disease occurs only rarely in the elderly.
Our case is considered to be one such rare case.
options: Unlikely to be causing an ADE

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is it that PSL is causing an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
In recent years, an increasing number of patients with connective tissue diseases have been treated with immunosuppressants in addition to steroids.
Recently, in our department, we encountered, in succession, tongue cancer and symptoms of hemorrhagic cystitis thought to have been triggered by cyclophosphamide during treatment for Sjogren syndrome and SLE.
Case 1: A 35-year-old woman.

Psoriasis vulgaris is an inflammatory keratinization disorder thought to develop when environmental factors such as stress, alcohol consumption, and smoking act on a genetic predisposition, but its association with colorectal cancer is unknown.
We report a case of synchronous multiple colorectal cancers arising in the cecum and sigmoid colon during treatment for psoriasis vulgaris.
[Case] A 60-year-old man.
[Chief complaint] Positive fecal occult blood test.
[History of present illness] The patient had had psoriasis vulgaris for 5 years and was receiving treatment with topical corticosteroids and adalimumab in the dermatology department of our hospital.
In September 2012, a positive fecal occult blood test prompted a detailed evaluation.
Colonoscopy revealed a type 0-IIa lesion in the cecum and a type 1 lesion in the sigmoid colon, and he was referred to the surgery department for surgery.
[Past medical history] Hypertension and hyperuricemia.
[Physical findings on admission] Height 159.5 cm, weight 66.1 kg, body temperature 35.6°C, blood pressure 149/99 mmHg, pulse 68 beats/min.
The abdomen was flat and soft, with no tenderness.
Erythema with scaling was observed predominantly on the face and trunk.
[Treatment course] Laparoscopy-assisted ileocecal resection and sigmoid colectomy were performed in January 2013.
The operation was performed using 5 ports, and reconstruction was performed with end-to-end anastomoses using FEEA and DST, respectively.
The operative time was 5 hours 49 minutes, and blood loss was 40 mL.
He was discharged on postoperative day 9.
No changes in the skin lesions were observed after surgery.
[Histopathological examination] The findings were C, type 0-IIa, pM, tub1 in adenoma, pN0, sH0, sP0, M0, fStage 0; and S, type 1, tub1, pSS, sN0, sP0, cM0, fStage II.
[Conclusion] At present, the association of psoriasis vulgaris or anti-TNF-α antibody therapy with the development of colorectal cancer is unknown, and further accumulation and examination of cases were considered necessary.
options: Unlikely to be causing an ADE

translation.question: How likely is it that the analgesic is causing an ADE (adverse event) in the following case report?
translation.text:
Case: A 48-year-old man.
He had steroid-dependent bronchial asthma with onset at age 41 and a history of a severe attack caused by an analgesic in March 1986 (aspirin-induced asthma).
He had been attending our outpatient department since June of that year.
In July 1989, anterior chest pain (hereafter ACP) developed after early-morning wheezing. Angina pectoris was suspected because nitroglycerin was effective.
Subsequently, chest pain almost completely disappeared with continued diltiazem treatment, but ACP occurred 2–3 times a year and was readily relieved by oral nitroglycerin.
BD inhalation therapy was initiated in June 1990 and continued, but ACP recurred in late November 1992.
On December 7, he visited the outpatient department for an early-morning asthma attack. After returning home, he developed severe ACP and returned to the outpatient department by ambulance.
His chest pain had almost resolved on arrival, but he was admitted that day because of bradycardia.
Although his PaO2 on admission was 77 Torr, his wheezing gradually worsened and improved with intravenous drip treatment with a bronchodilator and hydrocortisone.
At 9:30 AM on December 8, ACP recurred, and EKG showed ST elevation (II, III, aVF) and ST depression (V1–5).
Emergency cardiac catheterization was performed for suspected acute myocardial infarction, but no abnormalities were observed, and coronary vasospastic angina was diagnosed.
Similar chest pain developed on December 9, and intravenous heparin was effective.
Thereafter, his course was favorable with continuous intravenous infusions of heparin, nitrates, and PSL, and he was discharged on December 29.
Based on the above, asthma attacks are presumed to have contributed to coronary vasospasm in this case.
options: Unlikely to be causing an ADE

translation.question: How likely is it that L-OHP is causing an ADE (adverse event) in the following case report?
translation.text:
MSI is extensively involved in the development and progression of colorectal cancer, and MSI is considered to confer a better prognosis than non-MSI.
We report a case with both a BRAF mutation and MSI.
The patient was a 74-year-old woman.
Laparoscopy-assisted ileocecal resection (D3) and left supraclavicular lymph node biopsy were performed for cecal cancer with synchronous multiple lymph node metastases.
The diagnosis was C type 4 pSE pN3 H0 pP1 M1 (LYM), f Stage IV.
Postoperatively, treatment with mFOLFOX6, Bmab, and a peptide vaccine was initiated.
During cycle 6, she developed anaphylaxis due to L-OHP, and liver metastases also appeared, leading to an assessment of PD.
Treatment was switched from FOLFOX to FOLFIRI and continued.
After 4 cycles, the tumor reduction rate was 44%, and the response was assessed as PR.
However, at the same time, she developed interstitial pneumonia (IP) due to Bmab.
Furthermore, after resolution of IP, she developed small bowel perforation requiring emergency surgery.
Her postoperative course was favorable, but the tumor grew rapidly, and she died approximately 8 months after initial treatment.
BRAF-mutated tumors are generally resistant to anticancer agents, and the median OS has been reported to be approximately 10 months.
In this case, the tumor was resistant to first-line treatment but responded to second-line treatment.
However, IP and small bowel perforation developed during the treatment course, preventing adequate anticancer treatment, and the immunosuppressed state caused by steroid treatment for IP is also considered to have contributed to the shortened survival.
Had these events not occurred, she might have benefited from anticancer treatment.
Although there are scattered reports that the non-MSI group has a poor prognosis among cases with BRAF mutations, this case suggested the possibility of a response to treatment in the MSI group.
options: Unlikely to be causing the ADE

translation.question: How likely is UVB to have caused an ADE (adverse event) in the following case report?
translation.text:
The presence or absence of cutaneous malignancies was investigated in 229 patients with psoriasis who received topical PUVA therapy at Nagoya City University from 1970 to 1986.
Fifteen patients had died, but none of the deaths were due to cutaneous malignancies.
The surviving patients comprised 131 men and 83 women, aged 8–85 years (mean, 49.7).
The number of PUVA treatments received before the survey was 1–621 (106), and the total UVA irradiation dose was 1–6,718 J/cm² (459). Multiple basal cell epitheliomas were observed in one of these patients.
The patient was a 78-year-old man with psoriasis vulgaris.
He received topical PUVA therapy at Nagoya City University from 1976 to 1978.
Irradiation at the hospital totaled 96 sessions and 200 J/cm².
For the subsequent 10 years, he applied 0.3% 8MOP ointment topically and sunbathed at home.
Treatment consisted of sunbathing for 90 minutes starting at 10 a.m., 3–5 times per week.
The prescribed irradiation dose per session was UVA 6.8–14.3 J/cm² and UVB 0.3–0.9 J/cm².
He presented to Nagoya City University in September 1988.
The skin of the trunk and extremities showed marked atrophy and multiple PUVA lentigines.
Nine flat, elevated black papules measuring up to 3 mm in diameter were observed in the lower back and buttock region.
Histology showed superficial basal cell epithelioma.
There was no history of treatment with radiation or arsenic.
No cutaneous malignancies developed in the other 213 patients.
options: Unlikely to have caused the ADE

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is it that 5FU is causing an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
At our hospital, preoperative chemotherapy is frequently administered for Stage II–III esophageal cancer.
It is administered with the expectation of an effect on the primary lesion and lymph node metastases, but effects on secondary lesions such as IM, intraepithelial extension, and multiple lesions are also not uncommon.
We report a case in which the effect of preoperative chemotherapy made it possible to achieve a negative resection margin.
The patient was a 58-year-old man.
Endoscopy was performed for a chief complaint of impaired passage of food for 3 months, and an esophageal lesion was identified.
A type 3 lesion was observed in the Lt region and was diagnosed as cT3N2; however, a 0-IIa+IIc lesion was also observed proximally, 19 cm from the upper incisors, in the UtCe region, representing a coexisting T1bSM1 lesion in multifocal disease.
Two courses of preoperative chemotherapy consisting of CDDP 70 mg/m2 (day 1), Docetaxel 70 mg/m2 (day 1), and 5FU 700 mg/m2 (days 1–5) were administered, and the course was uneventful, with no serious adverse events.
Response assessment after 2 courses showed shrinkage of the primary lesion in the Lt region and the metastatic lymph nodes, but the response remained within the range of SD.
The 0-IIa+IIc lesion in the UtCe region showed shrinkage from the time of the first course and had disappeared after 2 courses.
Surgery was performed after chemotherapy.
Esophagectomy via right thoracotomy and laparotomy with gastric conduit reconstruction was performed, but the proximal resection margin was distal to this proximal lesion.
More than 1 year has passed since surgery, but no findings of recurrence have been observed in the residual esophagus.
This case was considered to suggest the possibility that chemotherapy may reduce the extent of resection.
options: Unlikely to be causing an ADE

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely are celecoxib and teprenone to have caused the ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
【Objective】To report a case of erythema multiforme-type drug eruption caused by celecoxib.
【Methods】The patient was a 66-year-old woman with a history of allergic rhinitis and hepatitis B.
From mid-December 2009, she took celecoxib and tebrenone prescribed by a local orthopedic clinic for arthritis of the right second finger.
In mid-January, on the day after she finished taking these medications, erythema appeared on her trunk, extremities, and other areas after she took an over-the-counter medication. As the erythema spread, she first visited our department 3 days after onset.
At the initial visit, numerous erythematous lesions and papules were observed on the trunk, extremities, and occipital region.
Initially, erythema multiforme exudativum due to a viral infection and a drug eruption due to the over-the-counter medication were considered.
【Results】The erythema resolved in approximately 1 week with oral prednisolone 10 mg/day, oral olopatadine hydrochloride, and topical diflucortolone valerate.
Subsequently, in early February, her joint pain recurred, and she took celecoxib and teprenone on her own. Several hours later, erythema appeared on her back, renal region, upper extremities, and other areas, along with edema of the lips. She visited our department the following day and was treated with oral prednisolone (tapered from 15 mg/day), oral olopatadine hydrochloride, and topical diflucortolone valerate. The erythema resolved in approximately 10 days.
Patch testing with celecoxib and teprenone was positive for celecoxib and negative for teprenone.
【Conclusion】Based on these findings, this case was diagnosed as an erythema multiforme-type drug eruption caused by celecoxib.
Nine cases of drug eruption caused by celecoxib have been reported in Japan since 2008, and we reviewed the literature, including our own case.
options: Unlikely to be causing the ADE

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is prednisolone to have caused an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
A 6-year-old girl.
Her past medical and family histories were unremarkable.
Painful erosions appeared in the oral cavity and on the lips around September 1989 (at age 5).
She was diagnosed with stomatitis by a local dentist and received treatment, but her symptoms worsened.
She was admitted to our department on March 28, 1990.
On admission, extensive erosions were observed on the oral mucosa and lips, and two small papules with surface erosions were present on the abdomen.
Biopsy of an abdominal skin lesion revealed cleft formation immediately above the basal layer of the epidermis and the presence of acantholytic cells. Direct immunofluorescence also revealed intercellular deposition of IgG and C3 in the epidermis.
On indirect immunofluorescence, the intercellular antibody titer was 1:640.
Based on these findings, pemphigus vulgaris was diagnosed.
Treatment was initiated with prednisolone 20 mg/day (1 mg/kg).
By day 5, the oral erosions had disappeared, and after 2 months, the intercellular antibody titer had decreased to 1:40.
There was no subsequent recurrence of the skin lesions, and no steroid-induced adverse effects were observed other than moon facies.
The prednisolone dose was gradually reduced, and she is currently receiving 5 mg/day.
This case is the first reported case in Japan of pemphigus with onset in a child aged 10 years or younger.
options: Unlikely to be causing an ADE

translation.question: How likely is cyclophosphamide to be causing ADEs (adverse events) in the following case report?
translation.text:
In recent years, an increasing number of patients with connective tissue diseases have been treated with immunosuppressants in combination with steroids.
Recently, in our department, we encountered successive cases of tongue cancer and symptoms of hemorrhagic cystitis thought to have been triggered by cyclophosphamide during treatment for Sjogren syndrome and SLE.
Case 1: A 35-year-old woman.
Despite administration of PSL for a diagnosis of Sjogren syndrome beginning in August 1985, annular erythema repeatedly appeared and disappeared.
In September 1989, administration of cyclophosphamide 25 mg was initiated.
In July of the following year, a squamous cell carcinoma appeared on the right lateral border of the tongue, measuring 21 × 10 mm and presenting as a milky-white, cauliflower-like elevated lesion with a central depression.
Case 2: A 19-year-old woman.
SLE developed in May 1979.
During PSL treatment, lupus nephritis was noted in 1987, and concomitant administration of cyclophosphamide 50 mg was initiated.
Around January 1990, marked anemia and hematuria developed, and hemorrhagic cystitis due to cyclophosphamide was suspected.
We reported these two cases and examined the administration of immunosuppressants in patients with connective tissue diseases, focusing on their adverse effects.

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is oral pazopanib to have caused an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
The patient was a 74-year-old woman.
She was receiving outpatient treatment at our hospital's department of obstetrics and gynecology for lung and splenic metastases from uterine leiomyosarcoma.
Oral pazopanib 800 mg was started on December 19, 201X, but blood tests on January 22, 201X+1 showed marked liver enzyme elevations of a mixed pattern, with T-Bil 7.85 mg/dl, D-Bil 5.07 mg/dl, AST 559 IU/L, ALT 515 IU/L, LDH 747 IU/L, and ALP 1490 IU/L, prompting consultation with our department.
Various autoantibodies and viral markers were negative.
DLST for pazopanib was negative.
Scoring according to the DDW-J 2004 drug-induced liver injury workshop yielded +2 for the interval to onset, +2 for the presence or absence of causes other than drugs, and +1 for previous reports of liver injury, for a total score of 5 points. Drug-induced liver injury due to pazopanib was suspected, and the plan was to discontinue administration and monitor the clinical course.
However, blood tests 1 week later showed a trend toward worsening liver function with a cholestatic pattern, with T-Bil 22.37 mg/dl, D-Bil 15.02 mg/dl, AST 447 IU/L, ALT 348 IU/L, LDH 499 IU/L, and ALP 2360 IU/L, so a liver biopsy was performed that day to investigate the cause.
Liver histology showed cholestasis in hepatocytes around the central veins, inflammatory cell infiltration predominantly consisting of small lymphocytes in the portal tracts, and focal hepatocellular necrosis within the lobules, leading to a diagnosis of drug-induced liver injury showing impaired bile transport and features of hepatitis.
Although the possibility of tumor progression was also considered, liver dysfunction was the predominant pathology, and steroid pulse therapy (500 mg/day) was started that day.
After 1 week, hepatobiliary enzyme levels showed a trend toward improvement, so the steroid dose was gradually reduced, and hepatobiliary enzyme levels normalized 2 months after administration was started.
Although sporadic reports of drug-induced liver injury due to pazopanib have also appeared in Japan, there are few reports in which a liver biopsy was performed for Grade 4 injury and a definitive diagnosis was reached, as in this case.
We encountered a case of drug-induced liver injury due to pazopanib that responded to steroid pulse therapy and report it here, incorporating our experience with this case.
options: Unlikely to be causing the ADE

translation.question: How likely is it that SOF/VEL is causing an ADE (adverse event) in the following case report?
translation.text:
[Objective] In early 2019, sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (SOF/VEL) became available for the first time in Japan for decompensated cirrhosis due to hepatitis C. While this provides more patients with an opportunity for viral eradication, these patients have many complications of cirrhosis, and greater attention than ever is considered necessary regarding the occurrence of adverse events during treatment.
Therefore, the objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of treatment in patients who were started on SOF/VEL at our hospital.
[Methods] We examined the clinical backgrounds and treatment courses of six patients with decompensated cirrhosis due to hepatitis C who were started on SOF/VEL at our hospital.
[Results] Of the six patients started on SOF/VEL, two were men and four were women.
The median age was 68 years (52–81 years).
All patients had Genotype 1b and no history of DAA treatment.
At the start of SOF/VEL, the Child-Pugh classification (CPS) score was 7 in two patients, 10 in two patients, 11 in one patient, and 15 in one patient. Four patients had a history of treatment for liver cancer, and two had esophageal varices before treatment initiation.
Two patients also had a history of encephalopathy, and five had ascites before administration.
All patients started treatment under inpatient management.
Serious adverse events occurred in three patients during treatment.
Case A was a 56-year-old man.
His CPS score was 10.
Esophageal varices had been identified two months before the start of administration but had not been treated.
Four weeks after starting SOF/VEL, he developed ruptured esophageal varices, for which hemostatic treatment was performed, and treatment was discontinued that same day.
HCV RNA became negative three weeks after the start of administration, but relapse occurred six weeks after discontinuation.
Case B was an 81-year-old woman.
Her CPS score was 10.
First-degree atrioventricular block had previously been noted, but echocardiography showed no abnormalities.
She developed sepsis due to cellulitis on the same day that SOF/VEL administration was started.
On the second day after administration, her eGFR decreased to 29.0, and sinus arrest also developed that same day, so treatment was discontinued. The sinus arrest improved the following day. Case C was a 52-year-old woman with a CPS score of 15. She had a history of hepatic encephalopathy.
She had chronic renal failure equivalent to stage 3b.
She developed grade IV hepatic encephalopathy in the first week after starting SOF/VEL, but showed a tendency toward improvement by the following day with fluid administration, and treatment was continued.
She subsequently developed a tendency toward fluid retention and developed atrial fibrillation and heart failure in week 3, but improved with diuretics. However, her eGFR gradually declined during the course, reaching 19.3 in week 6, so treatment was discontinued.
Liver failure progressed beginning 10 days after discontinuation of SOF/VEL, and she died 16 days after discontinuation.
Except for one patient who discontinued treatment early, HCV RNA became negative in five patients, and the two patients who completed treatment have achieved SVR4.
[Conclusion] Although SOL/VEL has high antiviral efficacy, patients with decompensated cirrhosis are prone to changes in their clinical condition, and utmost care is required in monitoring their course during treatment.
In particular, inpatient management is considered desirable early after treatment initiation.
options: Unlikely to be causing an ADE

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is it that the anti-PD-1 antibody is causing an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
The patient was a man in his 60s who was receiving Nivolumab 150 mg every 2 weeks as second-line treatment for laryngeal cancer in the Department of Otolaryngology at our hospital.
Blood tests 4 months after treatment initiation showed T-bil 0.81 mg/dl, AST 91 U/l, ALT 144 U/l, ALP 1478 U/l, and γGT 426 U/l, indicating liver injury with predominant elevation of biliary enzymes, and he was referred to the Department of Gastroenterology.
He had no subjective symptoms other than a fever of 37.6°C, and abdominal examination revealed no remarkable findings.
Blood biochemical testing was negative for various viral markers, ANA, and AMA2, and IgG and IgG4 were within normal ranges.
CT showed diffuse dilatation and wall thickening of the common bile duct and right and left hepatic ducts, as well as gallbladder enlargement and gallbladder wall thickening, but MRCP and ERC showed no strictures or neoplastic lesions in the bile ducts.
Liver histology showed no prominent inflammatory changes or necrosis of hepatocytes, but revealed infiltration of diverse inflammatory cells in the portal areas and focal findings of nonsuppurative destructive cholangitis.
Based on these findings, immune checkpoint inhibitor-related cholangitis was suspected, and Nivolumab was discontinued. However, biochemical and imaging findings did not improve, so PSL 30 mg was initiated.
Hepatobiliary enzyme levels gradually improved, but cholangitis worsened again when PSL was tapered to 15 mg, so UDCA 600 mg was added.
Cholangitis subsequently improved, and PSL was discontinued, leaving UDCA monotherapy.
A response had been achieved with Nivolumab, but the tumor worsened again after treatment interruption. Systemic chemotherapy with cytotoxic anticancer agents was administered but was ineffective. As there had been no recurrence of cholangitis during that time, Nivolumab was resumed following discussion, also in accordance with the patient's strong wishes.
More than 8 months have since elapsed without recurrence of liver dysfunction, and the tumor has begun to shrink again.
Reports of cholangitis as an immune checkpoint inhibitor-related adverse event (irAE) are rare, and there is currently no consensus regarding treatment.
It also remains unclear whether anti-PD-1 antibody treatment should be resumed or permanently discontinued after recovery from irAEs, including cholangitis.
We report, with a review of the literature, a rare case in which cholangitis improved with combined PSL and UDCA therapy and an anti-PD-1 antibody was readministered during UDCA monotherapy.
options: Unlikely to be causing an ADE

translation.question: In the following case report, how likely is it that Pembrolizumab is causing an ADE (adverse event)?
translation.text:
[Objective] Immune checkpoint inhibitors exert antitumor effects by inhibiting the immune system.
However, they are known to cause immune-related adverse events (immune related Adverse Effects: irAEs) in various organs, and fatal cases have also been reported.
Liver injury is a frequent irAE, and according to the package insert, liver injury and hepatitis together occur in approximately 10% of patients.
Liver biopsy shows findings resembling autoimmune hepatitis, but few reports are available.
We report a case of acute liver injury caused by Pembrolizumab.
[Case] The patient was a man in his 60s.
In November 201x, he was diagnosed with Stage 4 lung cancer with bone metastases.
Because PD-L1 expression was confirmed, pembrolizumab was initiated in December at a dose of 200 mg every 3 weeks.
At cycle 4, AST was 44 IU/L and ALT was 63 IU/L.
Blood tests at the time of cycle 5 showed AST of 120 IU/L and ALT of 176 IU/L, and treatment was discontinued. However, liver dysfunction subsequently worsened, and decreased appetite was also noted, leading to hospitalization.
Height was 163 cm and weight was 66 kg. No particular abnormalities were noted on abdominal examination.
On admission, AST was 1361 IU/L, ALT 1593 IU/L, T-Bil 1.1 mg/dL, IgG 1027 mg/dl, PT 81%, M2BPGi 1.06, and ANA titer 1:40; HCV antibody and HBsAg were negative.
Ultrasonography showed fatty liver, with no atrophy or ascites.
Histopathological findings showed extensive hepatocyte loss, hemorrhage, and infiltration of macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells around the central veins.
Spotty necrosis was observed within the lobules, and mild lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltration was observed in the portal areas.
After administration of Methylprednisolone 1000 mg for 3 days, AST decreased to 270 IU/L and ALT to 822 IU/L, showing a trend toward improvement.
Thereafter, prednisolone was initiated at 1 mg/kg/day and gradually tapered, and AST/ALT returned to the reference range after approximately 2 months.
[Discussion] One characteristic of immune checkpoint inhibitors is their sustained efficacy, with antitumor effects persisting for a long time after treatment discontinuation.
However, irAEs are also said to persist in the same manner.
In hepatocellular-type drug-induced liver injury, liver injury usually resolves rapidly after discontinuation of the causative drug, but with immune checkpoint inhibitors, some cases worsen after drug discontinuation.
In this case as well, liver enzymes rose rapidly even after drug discontinuation.
We consider it essential to perform an early liver biopsy to establish the diagnosis and then promptly initiate corticosteroids.
options: Unlikely to be causing an ADE
